21dma-structure TV script

As an intermediate-term swing trader, the 21-day moving average is the backbone of my system. Over time, I’ve simplified my approach to the point where this is really the only indicator I keep on my charts — aside from a few key lines to help define structure and pivots.

To give that moving average more context and flexibility, I use a 21-day EMA structure, built from the lows, highs, and closing prices. This creates a dynamic zone — not just a single line — that helps me visualize trend, momentum, and risk. It leaves room for natural volatility while keeping me anchored to the trend.

Everything I do — from entry to trimming to holding — revolves around this structure. When price is above it, I lean in. When it’s below and declining, I stay out or manage risk tighter. Simple, clean, and consistent.

My process starts with the market because the exact same setup can behave very differently depending on the environment. A clean breakout in a healthy market is not the same trade as a clean breakout when breadth is deteriorating, volatility is expanding, and risk appetite is fading.

Context changes everything.

Why I Trade Top-Down

Most traders start with the stock. They see a chart they like, notice a breakout or pullback, and then try to justify the trade.

I prefer to do the opposite.

Once I understand the market environment, I move down to sectors, industries, and themes. I want to know where capital is actually flowing, which areas are improving relative to others, and which groups are starting to separate from the rest of the market.

There is usually no reason to fight rotation when you can trade with it.

From there, I narrow the search to the strongest stocks inside those groups. I’m looking for names showing relative strength, good liquidity, constructive price structure, and the ability to hold gains when the broader market gets noisy.

The goal is not to own every stock in a strong theme. It is to find the best expression of that theme.

This is where I use ThemesLab inside TradersLab. It doesn’t just show me which themes are leading, emerging, fading, or losing momentum; it also surfaces the top 5 names in each theme, which immediately narrows the opportunity set.

From there, it can also identify the best setups based on my own criteria. Those filters are customizable, so instead of scanning everything manually, I’m essentially asking: which leaders, inside the right themes, are now meeting the conditions I personally care about?

That’s where it becomes much more useful than simply ranking themes. It helps move the process from "Where is the strength?" to where is the actual opportunity?

Only after those layers line up do I focus heavily on the individual setup. That might be a pullback into support, a volatility contraction, a reclaim, or a breakout from a tight structure.

This is where a lot of traders begin.

For me, it comes much later. https://t.co/oDIZI0y34o

The workflow is simple:
Market → Group / Theme → Leader → Setup → Execution

Each step removes noise and narrows the opportunity set. By the time I reach the individual stock, much of the filtering has already happened.

Execution is the final layer: entry, stop, sizing, and trade management. Those things matter, but perfect execution cannot turn a low-quality idea into a high-quality one.

I would much rather have a slightly imperfect entry in a strong leader, inside a strong group, in a supportive market than a perfect entry in a stock fighting everything around it.

ThemesLab is simply one of the tools I use to make that top-down process faster. The tool is useful, but the real edge is the framework behind it: start broad, identify where strength is building, narrow into the leaders, and then wait for the right setup.

The question I ultimately want to answer is not simply:
“Is this chart bullish?”

It is:
“Is this the right stock, in the right group, in the right market, at the right time?”

That is what top-down trading means to me.

This is also why I don’t think top-down analysis is really about prediction. I’m not trying to know exactly what happens next. I’m trying to stack probabilities.

If the market is healthy, the group is strengthening, the stock is leading, and the setup offers clean risk, I have several reasons to like the trade instead of relying on a single chart pattern.

9/ It also changes how I think about scanning. Looking through hundreds or thousands of random charts can feel productive, but without context it often creates more ideas than clarity.

A better question is not:
“What stocks look good?”

It is:
“Where is strength concentrated, and which stocks are leading it?”

That small change makes the process much more efficient.

$PLTR  is a good example of why I generally don’t like buying extended breakouts.

You can buy the breakout and be technically “right” on the bigger picture, but if price is already stretched off the rising 21-day EMA (or whatever moving average you use for execution), one normal pullback can immediately put you -5% in the red.

That’s why I prefer buying weakness into support and into a rising 21dma structure. Your SL is tight, and it gives the trade time to build a cushion before the next expansion. If I get ~2R, I can trim, de-risk the position, and let the rest work.

Then if the setup eventually fails and I get stopped, the overall trade can still end around breakeven or even with a small profit.

Same stock. Same trend. Very different trade depending on where you enter.

$HOOD Chain was a great moment for crypto, and a revealing one. 

When the largest retail broker in the world chose where to put 24/7 stocks, yield and DeFi for 120+ countries, it didn’t choose the chain that spent five years optimizing for the cheapest transaction. 

It chose Ethereum, via Arbitrum. That decision tells you what consumers, and the institutions building for them, actually optimize for.

Two chains made two different bets.

Solana bet that fees were the product. 

It got there by concentrating validator infrastructure, and the bill came on Aug 12: one data-center routing fault knocked 102 of 699 validators offline, 29% of stake, 33 minutes, 4.5pts from losing finality. 

One provider hosts 27% of stake, above the Foundation’s own 25% cap. The status page never logged it and still reads “100% uptime.” 

The economics were built the same way: 95% of H1 2025 revenue was priority fees and Jito tips, i.e. memecoin flow. That flow left, and network revenue fell 87% YoY in H1 2026. Solana still owns spot memecoin volume, but it was monetizing speculation and not finance.

Ethereum bet that settlement was the product and let execution move to chains you can own. 

That is exactly what Robinhood bought: 100ms blocks (vs ~400ms on Solana), 10M+ daily transactions two weeks after mainnet, tokenized US equities 24/7, Uniswap and Chainlink on day one, ETH as gas, its own sequencer and its own economics, all settling back to Ethereum.

Look at where the new DeFi is actually being built and the pattern is the same. Perp CLOBs, tokenized equities, prediction markets and RWAs are now the volume; perp DEXs alone clear $1T+ a month. 

Hyperliquid built its own chain. 
Lighter is a zk-rollup on Arbitrum. 
Polymarket sits on an ETH L2. 

Ethereum holds ~48% of all RWA value. 

None of it lives on a shared L1, because these products want their own execution layer and someone else’s settlement. 

You can’t spin up your own Solana. 
Ethereum sells precisely that.

And the settlement layer is getting faster and cheaper on its own: Glamsterdam this quarter brings ePBS and parallel execution via block-level access lists, a gas-limit floor of 200M (from 60M), mainnet transfers already sub-cent, then Hegotá with FOCIL. Part of those changes will allow the L1 to perceive more value from the current revenue split/burn from L2s as well.

Layer that on the deepest liquidity and stablecoin base in crypto.

So $SOL is squeezed from both sides: losing the institutional and RWA layer to $ETH’s L2 stack, and losing the trading layer to purpose-built venues like $HYPE and now $HOOD Chain.

What the consumer wanted was new products, yield, good UX, small fees, 24/7 markets and security. 

Right now that lives in the $ETH ecosystem, and builders know it: organisations like @ethlabs_org are making it easier to onboard and are shifting $ETH’s already dominant position by listening to the users and builders.

Many traders think trade management starts after they enter.

I think it starts with the entry itself.

If I buy near a rising 21dma/support area, I can usually define risk tightly, give the trade room to work, and potentially build a cushion before the next expansion.

If I chase after a strong move, the opposite happens: my stop is farther away, position size has to come down, and a perfectly normal pullback can immediately put me under pressure. That changes everything.

A good entry doesn’t just improve your R:R on paper. It makes the entire trade easier to manage emotionally and mechanically. This is also why I like trimming around 2R. Once I’ve paid myself and reduced risk, I can give the remaining position more room to become a bigger winner.

I don’t really care about fundamentals when I trade.

Not because they’re useless, but because I believe most of what matters eventually gets expressed through price action, relative strength, group leadership, volume, and the market’s reaction.

A company can have great fundamentals and still be a terrible trade if the stock is weak, the group is lagging, and nobody is rewarding the story. On the other hand, when a stock is outperforming, its group is leading, price keeps respecting a rising structure, and institutions appear to be accumulating it, that already tells me something important is happening.

I don’t necessarily need to know every reason why.

Fundamentals explain the business. Price tells me whether the market currently cares.

As a trader, that second part matters a lot more to me.

The High-Probability Pullback Checklist
1-Scan
Stock appears in at least one of these scans.
-Near 10% 52WH
-3/6 Month High
-30% in 3 month

2-Trend
-Prior advance of 30%+.
-Stock is in Stage 2.
-Key EMAs are rising.

3-Pullback Depth
-Pullback is 30-40% of the prior advance.
-Avoid deeper corrections.

4-Location
-Price is between 11 DEMA and 51 DEMA.
-Preferred 21DEMA

5-Character
-Tight, linear price bars.
-Volume dries up into the pullback low.

6-Trigger
-Presence of a Demand Tail, IB, NR candles
- 3 Entry Tactics near Range candle.

7-Risk
-Stop-loss below the trigger low.
-Maximum stop distance within 3-5%.

8-Position Size
-Position size is based on entry price, sl distance
-Max Portfolio risk per position 1%
